outputs.L1:
Because the original text is a deeply evocative poem about waiting near a hospital, "polishing" it requires enhancing its literary cadence and clarity while preserving its poignant tone and all original details. 

Here are two options depending on how you intend to present the text:

### Option 1: Formatted as Polished Poetic Verse (Recommended)
*This option maintains the poetic structure and rhythm, enhancing punctuation, diction, and flow.*

> Praise the restless beds.  
> Praise the beds that do not adjust—  
> that will not lift the head to feed,  
> nor lower for injections or blood,  
> nor rise to watch the tinny TV.  
> 
> Praise the hotel television that refuses to quit its low murmur and holler.  
> Praise the room service that does not exist—  
> only the slow delivery to the front desk  
> of cooling pizzas and brown paper bags, leaky, greasy, and translucent.  
> 
> Praise the vending machines. Praise the loose change.  
> Praise the hot water, the steady heat,  
> or the loud, cool air that lulls the helpless to sleep.  
> 
> Praise the front desk clerk who remembers to wake Room 120  
> the moment the hospital rings.  
> Praise the silent phone.  
> Praise the darkness drawn by thick daytime curtains  
> after long nights spent waiting, awake.  
> 
> Praise the waiting—and then praise the nothing,  
> that quiet space so much better than bad news.  
> Praise the wake-up call at six in the morning; praise sleeping in.  
> Praise the sign hung on the doorhandle like a whisper,  
> like lips pressed silently shut.  
> 
> Praise the stranger's hands that strip away the sweat of the sheets.  
> Praise checking out.  
> Praise going home to beds left unmade for days—  
> beds that will not resurrect or rise,  
> but lie there as a child ought to sleep:  
> peaceful, tubeless, intact.  
> 
> Praise this beautiful mess that can finally be left behind.

---

### Option 2: Formatted as Elegant Literary Prose
*This option weaves the text into seamless, eloquent paragraphs suitable for an essay or narrative piece.*

> Praise the restless beds—the beds that refuse to adjust, that will not lift the head for feeding, lower for injections or blood draws, nor rise to view the tinny television. Praise the hotel TV that never ceases its low murmur and holler, and praise the non-existent room service, manifested only in the slow delivery to the front desk of cooling pizzas and brown paper bags, greasy, translucent, and leaking. Praise the vending machines and the loose change. Praise the hot water, the ambient heat, or the loud cool air that finally lulls the weary to sleep.
> 
> Praise the front desk staff who know to alert Room 120 the moment the hospital calls. Praise the blessedly silent phone. Praise the darkness drawn close by heavy daytime curtains after long, sleepless nights of vigil. Praise the agonizing wait, and then praise the nothingness—that silence so much better than bad news. 
> 
> Praise the six o'clock wake-up call, and praise the luxury of sleeping in. Praise the card hung on the doorknob like a whisper, like lips pressed silently shut. Praise the stranger’s hands that strip away the sweat-soaked sheets. Praise the act of checking out, and praise returning home to beds left unmade for days—beds that neither elevate nor resurrect, but lie still, just as a child ought to sleep: tubeless and at peace. Praise this mess, at last, that can be left behind.
outputs.L2:
Here is a complete rewrite of the text, maintaining every detail while utilizing prose structure and alternate phrasing:

Express gratitude for uncomfortable, motionless mattresses—the kind that lack motorized controls to tilt a body upright for dining, lower it for blood draws or injections, or incline it toward a low-quality television. Offer thanks for the motel TV that blares and hums endlessly, and for the absence of room service, where dining consists solely of retrieving lukewarm pizza and oil-stained, leaking paper sacks brought slowly to the lobby. Honor the snack dispensers, the spare coins, the scalding tap water, and the climate units—whether blasting warmth or loudly blowing cold air—that finally allow the exhausted to rest.

Give praise to the reception staff who remember to contact Room 120 the moment the medical center calls. Appreciate the unringing telephone and the dense window drapes that create artificial darkness during the day after a long, sleepless night of waiting. Bless the anxious waiting itself, and celebrate the total absence of updates, which remains far preferable to tragic news. 

Be thankful for the 6:00 AM wake-up call, the chance to oversleep, and the silence sign hanging from the doorknob like a muted whisper. Express appreciation for the anonymous housekeeper who swaps out the sweat-soaked linens. Finally, celebrate paying the bill and returning home to mattresses left messy for days—ordinary beds without mechanical lifts that lie quiet and tubeless, like a healthy resting child. Give thanks for this household clutter that can simply be left behind.
outputs.L3:
There is a strange, profound gratitude that comes from sinking into an ordinary hotel bed. After spending grueling hours in a hospital—surrounded by the sterile glare of fluorescent lights, the ominous hum of monitoring machinery, and rigid beds equipped with terrifying remotes, buttons, and metal rails—a standard mattress becomes a sacred sanctuary. In a simple hotel room, a bed is just a bed. It is not a medical instrument designed for crisis, but a soft, unpretentious place meant entirely for rest.

During such a prolonged and anxious ordeal, essential comfort is often found in the most mundane conveniences. A thick set of blackout curtains that can completely shut out the relentless morning sun, a box of greasy takeout eaten straight from the container, or the quiet trip down the hall to a vending machine for a cold soda become lifesavers. These small, unscripted moments provide a crucial anchor of normalcy when everything else in life feels wildly out of control.

In this temporary life between the hospital and the hotel, time moves differently. Every second spent watching a silent phone is heavy with anticipation, yet one quickly learns to value those quiet spans of waiting. In a medical crisis, silence is a shield; receiving no news, as agonizing as the suspense can be, is infinitely preferable to the sudden, sharp jolt of bad news. The quiet hours mean that things are stable, and that the doctors are simply doing their work.

The hotel environment itself offers a subtle, hands-off kind of care that an exhausted caregiver desperately needs. Behind a locked door, away from round-the-clock vital checks and shift changes, there is absolute privacy. Returning to a room where a housekeeper has quietly made the bed and refreshed the towels feels like an unexpected act of grace. When all of your physical and emotional energy is consumed by holding a vigil for a loved one, allowing the world to briefly take care of your basic environment is an incredible relief.

Ultimately, the true victory lies in leaving this sanctuary behind. The long, agonizing journey culminates in the immense relief of checking out, handing over the plastic keycards, and stepping out into the sunshine. Loading the car to return home—with a healthy, tubeless child resting safely in the back seat—transforms the hotel from a place of anxious exile into the final stepping stone toward healing and home.
outputs.L4:
Time moves differently in the shadow of a pediatric ward. Minutes stretch into agonizing, elasticity-defying hours, measured not by the ticking of a clock, but by the rhythmic beep of heart monitors, the hiss of artificial oxygen, and the agonizing void between medical updates. When you are waiting to hear if your child’s body will fight its way back, the sterile air of a hospital room becomes suffocating. 

Unable to bear the quiet terror of the waiting room any longer, I stepped out of the hospital’s glass doors and retreated to a budget hotel just across the concrete plaza. 

That hotel room became my unexpected sanctuary. In the face of catastrophic uncertainty, I found myself offering up a silent prayer of gratitude for its utterly aggressive normalcy. I praised the faint smell of stale carpet, the low, warm glow of a bedside lamp with a tilted shade, and the gentle, dull thrum of the wall-unit air conditioner. There were no heart-rate telemetry screens here. No antiseptic smells, no squeaking rubber soles of doctors hurrying down linoleum hallways, no hushed tones discussing red blood cell counts. The room was aggressively, beautifully mundane. I sat on the edge of a stiff polyester bedspread, clutching a paper cup of lukewarm, terrible coffee, and drew comfort from a world that was stubbornly, indifferent to my personal crisis. 

My phone rested in the palm of my hand like a live grenade. Every buzz sent a jolt of adrenaline through my chest. But as the hours dragged on, the silence from the hospital began to morph from terrifying to merciful. 

Then, the call finally came. 

"No news is good news," the nurse’s voice crackled through the speaker, warm and reassuring. "He’s stable. In fact, he’s doing so well we’re pulling the tubes. You can come bring him home."

The exhale that escaped me felt like it had been trapped in my lungs for days. 

The drive home was a blur of tears and sunlit asphalt. Walking through the doors of the hospital room to find my child—free of wires, IVs, and plastic tubing, his cheeks flushed with natural warmth—was a miracle wrapped in simple flesh and bone. 

Back at our house, the perspective shift was absolute. Before the hospital, I would have stressed over the state of the living room: the trail of plastic action figures scattered across the rug, the crust of dried oatmeal on the kitchen counter, the sticky handprints smudging the sliding glass door. 

Now, standing in the middle of that domestic chaos, holding my healthy child, I saw those imperfections for what they truly were: proof of life. The noise, the clutter, and the messy unpredictability of an ordinary day were no longer chores to be managed. They were a profound, magnificent blessing—the vibrant contrast to the cold, quiet precision of a hospital room we were lucky enough to leave behind.
outputs.L5:
We live in a world that constantly demands our movement. We spend our waking hours chasing validation, striving for excellence, and waiting for the sweet reward of praise—from managers, peers, loved ones, and society at large. Yet, when the noise of the day subsides, we retreat to a quiet, often overlooked sanctuary that deserves the highest praise of all: the bed.

There is a subtle poetry in the way a bed anchors a human life. It is both our starting line and our finish line. The simple, daily ritual of making one’s bed has earned praise from modern philosophers and military leaders alike, celebrated as the first small victory of the day. Completing that single task creates a tiny island of order in a chaotic world, proving that even before we step out the door, we are capable of accomplishment. 

Out in the public sphere, praise is conditional. It must be earned through productivity, charm, or talent. But the bed offers an unconditional acceptance that no audience can match. It demands no credentials and asks for no performance. Whether we return home carrying the heavy weight of failure or the light triumph of success, the bed receives us with the same yield of soft linen and steady support. It is the place where we digest the applause of the day—or lick the wounds of its absence.

Moreover, the bed is where the most intimate forms of praise are exchanged. It is where whispered words of affection are spoken in the dark, free from the judgment of the outside world. It is where a parent tucks in a child, offering warm encouragement before sleep. And, perhaps most importantly, it is the space where we learn to offer praise to ourselves. Lying beneath the blankets in the quiet dark, we finally have the space to reflect, breathe, and acknowledge our own quiet resilience.

We sing praises to grand cathedrals, soaring skyscrapers, and monuments of stone, yet it is the humble bed that cradles our existence. It holds us through our dreams, restores us when we are broken, and prepares us to face another day of striving. In the grand architecture of human survival and comfort, the bed stands supreme—a daily destination truly worthy of our deepest praise.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary praise poem in free verse about the experience of staying in a cheap motel while waiting for news from a hospital, using repeated "Praise..." litanies.
counterfactuals.output:
Praise the flickering *VACANCY* sign, its buzzing 'N'
a low, steady hymn against the damp highway air.
Praise the keycard that takes three swipes to green-light the door.
Praise the laminate floor, cold beneath bare feet,
and the faint, persistent ghost of pine cleaner, bleach, and old tobacco.

Praise the stiff polyester duvet, patterned in forgotten teal,
thick enough to wear like armor against the three a.m. chill.
Praise the wood-veneered nightstand, scarred by someone else’s hot coffee,
holding the cell phone face-down like a hand of unplayed cards.
Praise the black glass screen, silent and terrifyingly still,
holding its breath alongside me.

Praise the ice machine down the hall, its periodic avalanche 
crashing into the plastic tub, counting off the hours 
when the digital clock on the wall refuses to move.
Praise the hum of the mini-fridge vibrating through the headboard.
Praise the eighteen-wheelers shifting gears on the bypass,
carrying gravel, carrying timber, carrying all the ordinary world 
that keeps moving while mine has come to a halt.

Praise the styrofoam cup melting slightly around bad instant coffee.
Praise the bathroom mirror lit by a single flickering tube,
showing a face I barely recognize, drawn and washed out in gray.
Praise the muted TV casting its pale blue glow across the popcorn ceiling,
selling non-stick pans to a room full of shadows.

Praise the lungs that keep expanding without asking,
in and out, in and out,
doing the quiet, automatic work that two miles away,
beneath the harsh white halogens of the ICU,
a machine or a prayer is trying to teach yours to remember.

Praise the sanctuary of this liminal space, this two-star purgatory,
where no one knows my name, where no one asks for progress.
Praise the silence before the ring.
Praise the terrifying mercy of one more minute of *before*.

Praise the first thin smudge of gray pulling back the heavy drapes.
Praise the plastic blinds letting the morning through like a blade.
Praise the phone as it finally shudders against the wood—
praise the breath I take before I pick it up,
praise the heart that keeps beating in the dark,
praise whatever mercy is left on the fourth floor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem from the perspective of a parent staying in a hotel next to a children's hospital? Make it about the sensory details of the room, the agonizing wait for a phone call, and the ultimate relief of getting to take their child home.
counterfactuals.output:
The sheets smell of bleach and industrial thread,
A sterile attempt to mask lingering dread.
The carpet is patterned in muted maroon,
A labyrinth traced by the light of the moon.
I pace out its geometry, step after step,
Guarding the vigil that daylight once kept.

The window reveals what I’m trying to face:
A glass-and-steel giant across the street space.
The red glowing cross on the hospital tower
Casts a faint crimson wash on this room by the hour.
Inside that bright fortress, behind window four,
My heart is asleep on a third-floor layout floor.

Sensory details intrude on the night:
The buzz of the mini-fridge humming its light,
The dry, biting cold of the unit’s air-blow,
The screech of a car on the pavement below.
On the counter, a paper-wrapped cup sits untasted,
Beside instant coffee whose dark grounds were wasted.
Everything here is designed to forget,
A room built for transit, not holding regret.

And then, there’s the phone on the nightstand’s dark wood.
I’ve stared at its plastic as long as I could.
A glossy black block, heavy, silent, and cold,
Holding the answer I’m desperate to hold.
Every minute stretches out, forty miles wide,
As I count every breath that I’m keeping inside.
The digital clock flashes red: *four-fourteen*.
The quietest agony I’ve ever seen.

I imagine the doctors in ocean-green scrubs,
The rhythm of monitors, IV bag hubs,
The tiny, soft hand that I held until three,
Before they insisted on sending home me.

Then—
It breaks.
A sudden, electric, sharp ring cuts the air.
The room spins around me; I drop to my chair.
My fingers are trembling, slick with my sweat,
This moment, the scariest I’ve encountered yet.

"Hello?" I whisper, my voice paper-thin.
A breath on the line... then the words tumble in.
*"They’re awake. They are stable. The fever has flown.*
*Come over and pack them. You’re taking them home."*

The walls of the hotel room suddenly yield,
The air in my chest expands like a field.
The smell of the bleach is swallowed by dawn,
The dark, heavy shadow is suddenly gone.

I don't leave a tip, I don't smooth out the bed,
I slam shut the suitcase and rush out instead.
Out past the lobby, out into the air,
Leaving behind every terror and care.
Across the wet asphalt, I run to the door,
To the child who is waiting on that third floor.
No more sterile rooms, no more waiting alone—
We’re checking out now. 
We are going back home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a litany poem honoring the mundane objects in a hotel room during a family medical crisis—vending machines, loud AC, greasy takeout, blackout curtains—and the gratitude when no bad news comes.
counterfactuals.output:
Praise be to the beige sanctuary of Room 214.
Praise the thin carpet, worn down by a thousand strangers’ anxious pacing.
Praise the keycard that chirped its small, green light of permission.

Blessed be the air conditioner, clanking and cruel in the corner,
blessed be its metallic shudder, its violent cough of frost,
its roar that doused the ghost-sound of ICU monitors,
its roar that drowned the ambulances carving up the midnight street.
Blessed be its mechanical racket, a wall built against our thoughts.

Praise the glowing vending machine in the alcove near the ice,
a fluorescent altar humming in the dark.
Praise coil C6 for dropping its bag of salty, stale chips,
praise the crumpled five-dollar bill smoothed flat against a thigh,
praise the cheap chocolate eaten at 2:00 a.m. out of sheer obligation,
the sugar and sodium keeping the trembling body tethered to the earth.

Blessed be the greasy paper bag of midnight takeout,
blessed be the lukewarm fries and the styrofoam sweating condensation.
Blessed be the plastic fork that snapped in the container,
the salt on our fingers, the heavy, unholy comfort of fat and oil
eaten off the laminate desk, without hunger, without taste,
just fuel poured into an engine that was afraid to stop running.

Praise the blackout curtains, heavy as a seal,
praise their rubbery backing and the plastic clip that held them pinched shut.
Praise the darkness they defended,
holding the sun at bay, refusing to let the morning enter
until we were ready to face whatever the morning carried.
Praise the artificial night that allowed us to hide.

Blessed be the scratchy polyester bedspread we did not pull down.
Blessed be the bad coffee in the tiny paper cups.
Blessed be the TV playing a sitcom we did not watch,
its laugh track filling the hollow spaces between our prayers.

Most of all, praise the black landline phone beside the bed.
Praise its long, unbroken silence through the terrible hours.
Praise the 4:00 a.m. that passed without a ring.
Praise the 6:00 a.m. that brought only the grey rim of ordinary light.

Praise the cell phone buzzing on the nightstand—not with a doctor’s gravity,
but with a weary, miraculous text: *Stable. You can come back now.*

Praise the breath released into the cheap hotel air.
Praise the packing of the bags.
Praise the incredible, holy mercy
of an ordinary morning,
and leaving this room behind.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a modern psalm, comparing hospital beds to motel beds and home beds, ending with the image of a child sleeping safely without tubes.
counterfactuals.output:
Lord, you have measured my lying down and my rising up,
yet I have rested in three different kingdoms of the night.

I have known the hospital bed, 
that altar of vinyl, steel, and harsh fluorescent grace.
It is a bed of numbers, where breath is counted by a machine,
where mercy arrives in silver needles and plastic bags,
and the sheets are bleached so white they erase the sun.
Here, we do not sleep; we surrender.
We lie awake to the rhythm of the monitor’s frantic hymn,
praying for the dawn to bring a better standard.

And I have known the motel bed,
the transient purgatory of the exhausted.
Its blanket is thin, smelling of old dust and highway light,
sagging beneath the weight of those who are far from peace.
It is the bed of the waiting—
where parents collapse with their shoes still on,
listening through the dark for a phone call from the third floor,
trapped between the terror of staying and the terror of going home.

Neither of these is the sanctuary You promised.
For the home bed is built of quiet mercy.
It holds the scent of washed cotton and familiar rain;
it accepts the weary without asking for a chart or a key.

Deliver us, O God, from the rooms of wire and neon.
Lead us back to the wooden frames of our own making.

Let the final grace be this:
To walk into the soft shadows of a quiet hallway,
and stand at the doorway of a small room.
To look down at a child, fast asleep in a wooden bed,
tucked beneath a faded quilt.

No clear plastic lines tracing their skin,
no harsh tape binding their wrists,
no hum of oxygen filling the quiet air—

Only the slow, sweet, unassisted rise and fall of a chest,
breathing the room’s plain air,
held safely in the dark,
and completely restored.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a raw, emotional free-verse poem about the relief of checking out of a motel after a long hospital vigil and going home.
counterfactuals.output:
The keycard is a cheap piece of white plastic,
light as a bird’s skull,
but it has weighed fifty pounds in my pocket 
for fourteen straight days.

Room 208 smelled of stale smoke, lemon disinfectant,
and the sharp, cold edge of panic.
Fourteen nights I lay on that scratchy, yellowing quilt,
staring at the water stain on the ceiling,
my ears ringing with phantom telemetry beeps—
that rhythmic, fragile pulse 
that was keeping my world from snapping in half.

I am so tired of Styrofoam cups.
Tired of bad coffee that tastes like tin.
Tired of the fluorescent purgatory of the ICU waiting room,
the plastic chairs that bruise your spine,
the doctors who talk in careful, terrifying sentences 
that always begin with *if*.

My skin feels coated in hospital soap and sweat.
My bones feel like wet chalk. 

But this morning, the doctor smiled.
A real smile. Not the gentle, pitying kind.
He gave us the green light.
He gave me back my life.

I toss the keycard onto the laminate front desk.
The clerk doesn't ask how my stay was.
He sees the dark, bruised moons under my eyes,
the way I’m gripping my canvas duffel like a survivor holding a liferaft.
"Drive safe," he says softly.

The glass doors slide open and the outside air hits me—
not filtered, not chilled, not smelling of iodine—
just cold, messy, wild air.
I inhale until my ribs ache with it. 

I unlock the car. 
I don't turn on the radio.
I just turn the wheel away from the brick tower,
away from the helipad,
away from the place where we almost lost everything.

The highway unfurls, and for the first time in two weeks,
my shoulders drop an inch. Then two.
My knuckles stop turning white on the steering wheel.

When I put the key into my own front door,
the house smells of dry wood, old books, and home.
The quiet inside isn't a threat anymore. 
It’s just quiet.

I drop the bag on the floor.
I drop my shoes.
I collapse onto the middle of my own bed,
pull the heavy blanket over my head,
and finally, 
finally,
I cry—
not because the world is ending,
but because it didn't.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
